templates.title: Invitation acceptance within 14 days, by sender region and month
templates.subtopic: gaps-and-islands with LAG and a running sum, as-of joins, inclusive interval windows

sections.scenario: A professional network's growth team watches how often connection invitations are accepted, by the sender's region, to spot regions where invitations go unanswered. The report is an aggregate: it never lists who invited whom. Senders can withdraw an invitation, and they sometimes send the same member another one later; the team wants one row per invitation a member actually had in front of them, not one per click.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns month, region, invitations, accepted_14d, acceptance_rate, one row per calendar month (UTC, as the first day of the month, a date) of the invitation's first send and the sender's region, ordered by month, region. invitations counts invitations whose outcome is not withdrawn; accepted_14d counts those whose outcome is accepted with status_at no more than 14 days after the invitation's first send (exactly 14 days counts); acceptance_rate is accepted_14d / invitations rounded to 4 decimal places. {{resend_rule}} {{region_rule}} {{floor_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). invitations has {{invitation_rows}} rows: one per send, with the send's final status (pending, accepted, ignored or withdrawn) and the time it reached it (status_at, NULL while pending). invitation_id is not in time order.
sections.assumptions: Members, regions, the resend limit and every count are hypothetical; the resend and withdrawal rules are this exercise's rules, not a description of any product's limits (check current docs). All timestamps are UTC.
sections.criteria: Withdrawn outcomes removed before counting; the 14-day window inclusive and measured from the first send; months of the first send in UTC; (Hard+) resends collapsed by a gap rule into one invitation with the latest send's outcome, a later invitation beyond the limit counted separately, and the floor applied after withdrawals; (Very Hard) the region as of the first send; correct rounding and deterministic order; output stays aggregate; can discuss incomplete windows, small groups and incremental recomputation.

clarifications.q: Which month does an invitation belong to?
clarifications.a: The UTC month of its first send, even if it was resent or accepted in the next month.

clarifications.q: Is "within 14 days" inclusive?
clarifications.a: Yes. status_at <= first send + 14 days; one second later is too late.

clarifications.q: Does an ignored or pending invitation count?
clarifications.a: Yes, in invitations and not in accepted_14d. Only withdrawn outcomes leave the denominator.

clarifications.q: If an earlier send was withdrawn and the resend was accepted, what is the outcome?
clarifications.a: The status of the latest send in the chain: accepted.

clarifications.q: Can I output member ids to check my work?
clarifications.a: While debugging, yes; the deliverable is the aggregate only.

hints: Order each sender–recipient pair's sends with LAG(sent_at); a send that is the pair's first, or more than the resend limit after the previous send, starts a new invitation.
A running SUM of that "starts a new invitation" flag numbers the invitations; group by it to get the first send and the latest send's status.
Look up the region with a correlated subquery or LATERAL … ORDER BY valid_from DESC LIMIT 1 at the first send, then apply the floor with HAVING.
followups: The team wants the same rate by the recipient's region instead. Which joins change, and does anything about withdrawn invitations change?
Invitations sent in the last 14 days have not had their full window yet. How would you keep this month's number from looking artificially low on a live dashboard?
A region has 40 invitations in a month. How would you show its rate without implying more precision than it has?
At billions of invitations a year, how would you compute this incrementally each day, given that a resend can change last week's invitation?

rules.ask: Your ranking finds each pair's sends in order. How do you decide where one invitation ends and the next begins?
The same member was invited again two months later. Is that one invitation or two in your query?
A sender moved region after sending. Which region should their August invitation count for?
An acceptance exactly 14 days after the send: does your comparison count it?
Is the regional rate the average of each sender's rate, or the ratio of the totals? Which one does the team want?

templates.title: Company page follower growth per week, with quick refollows collapsed
templates.subtopic: LEAD and LAG pairing, a calendar spine with generate_series, end-of-window filters

sections.scenario: Company page admins on a professional network see how many followers their page gained each week. Members sometimes unfollow a page and follow it again a few days later (a mis-tap, or a cleanup of their feed), and the admins have said those round trips make the weekly numbers look noisy. The product rule for this report (this exercise's rule; check current docs): a quick round trip is not growth or loss, and small pages are left out of this report.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns page_id, week_start, follows, unfollows, net_new for the {{weeks}} weeks starting Monday {{first_week}} (week_start is the Monday of each week, a date; weeks run Monday 00:00 to Sunday 23:59:59 UTC). Count follow and unfollow events per page and week, and net_new = follows - unfollows. An unfollow followed by the same member's next event on the same page being a follow no more than 7 days later (exactly 7 days included) is a quick round trip: drop both events. Report every week of the window for each reported page, with zeros where nothing counted. Report only pages whose follower count at the end of the window — followers_at_start plus all follows minus all unfollows in the log — is at least {{min_followers}}. Order by page_id, week_start. {{dup_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). follow_events has {{event_rows}} rows, all inside the window; for each member and page the events alternate between follow and unfollow (after duplicates are removed). event_id is not in time order.
sections.assumptions: Pages, members, the floor of {{min_followers}} followers and the 7-day rule are hypothetical. The report is per page and never lists who followed. followers_at_start is the count just before {{first_week}}.
sections.criteria: Round trips found by pairing each unfollow with the same member's next event on the page; inclusive 7-day bound (Hard+); both events dropped even across a week boundary; a complete week spine with zeros; the floor applied to the end-of-window count; (Very Hard) duplicate deliveries removed before pairing and repeated cycles handled; Monday weeks in UTC; deterministic order; output is per page, never per member.

clarifications.q: A round trip that starts on a Sunday and ends on Monday — which week loses a follower?
clarifications.a: Neither. Both events are dropped, wherever they fall.

clarifications.q: What about a follow followed by a quick unfollow?
clarifications.a: That is a real follow and a real unfollow; both count. Only unfollow-then-refollow is collapsed.

clarifications.q: Does collapsing change the floor?
clarifications.a: No. A round trip nets to zero, so the end-of-window count is the same with or without it.

clarifications.q: Should a page with no events in some week still have a row for it?
clarifications.a: Yes, with zeros, for every week of the window.

clarifications.q: Is the floor checked at the start of the window?
clarifications.a: No, at the end: followers_at_start plus the window's net change.

hints: Use LEAD(event_type) and LEAD(event_at) over each (page, member) ordered by time to find unfollows that are undone, and LAG to find the refollows that undo them.
Build the week list with generate_series and CROSS JOIN it with the eligible pages before the LEFT JOIN to events.
DATE_TRUNC('week', event_at) returns the Monday in PostgreSQL; compare it with the spine as a date.
followups: Admins in Tokyo want their weeks to start on Monday in their own time zone. What changes, and what happens to an event at 23:30 UTC on a Sunday?
The log can be delivered late by up to two days. How would you publish this week's number before then, and how would you correct it?
The rule changes to collapse round trips within 30 days. Which weeks of last quarter's published report would change, and how do you communicate that?
At millions of pages, how would you maintain this report incrementally instead of rescanning the log every day?

rules.ask: How does your join pick the refollow that belongs to an unfollow, rather than a later one?
Your LEAD looks at the next event. What happens when the same member does two round trips in a row?
Where does the list of weeks come from, and would your query still return a week in which no page had any events?
Do you check the floor against the start or the end of the window, and why does that matter for a page that is shrinking?
What exactly makes two rows duplicates here, and could DISTINCT ever remove two genuinely different events?

templates.title: Recruiter message response rate per seat, bulk duplicates collapsed
templates.subtopic: gaps-and-islands chains, first-event lookups across a group, as-of cutoffs

sections.scenario: Recruiters on a professional network message members from a paid seat, and a seat's response rate is shown to the recruiter's admin as a measure of outreach quality. Members can accept, decline or reply; a decline is still an answer, and the product counts it as one (this exercise's rule; check current docs). Bulk sends sometimes reach the same member more than once, and those copies should not make a seat look worse or better.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns seat_id, messages, responses_7d, response_rate, one row per seat with at least one counted message, ordered by seat_id. Messages from the same seat to the same member form a duplicate group when each is sent no more than {{dup_hours}} hours after the previous one (exactly {{dup_hours}} hours included); the group counts as one message, kept at its earliest sent_at. A response is an accepted, declined or replied event (delivered and read are not). responses_7d counts kept messages whose first response came no more than 7 days after the kept sent_at (exactly 7 days counts); response_rate is responses_7d / messages rounded to 4 decimal places. {{copy_rule}} {{asof_rule}} {{chain_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). messages has {{message_rows}} rows; message_events holds the delivery, read and response events. Ids are not in time order. Message content is not in the data and is not needed.
sections.assumptions: Seats, members, the {{dup_hours}}-hour duplicate limit and every number are hypothetical. Timestamps are UTC. The rate is about a seat's outreach and is shown only in aggregate.
sections.criteria: Duplicate groups by a chained gap rule (inclusive) with the earliest copy kept; declines counted and reads not; the first response across all copies, timed from the kept message, inclusive 7-day bound (Hard+); the as-of cutoff on the kept message, from the stated as-of time rather than the clock (Hard+); (Very Hard) three-copy chains and multiple response events; correct rounding; deterministic order; per-seat output only.

clarifications.q: Is a decline a response?
clarifications.a: Yes. Accepting, declining and replying are all responses; a read is not.

clarifications.q: Three copies arrive 5, 5 and 5 hours apart with a 6-hour limit. One group or two?
clarifications.a: One: each copy is within the limit of the previous one.

clarifications.q: Which copy's time starts the 7 days?
clarifications.a: The kept (earliest) copy's sent_at.

clarifications.q: Is a seat with messages but no responses reported?
clarifications.a: Yes, with responses_7d = 0.

clarifications.q: Should the output include members or messages?
clarifications.a: No. One row per seat.

hints: Number duplicate groups with LAG(sent_at) per (seat, member) and a running SUM of "more than the limit after the previous message".
Map every message to its group, then take MIN(event_at) of response events across all of the group's messages.
Apply the as-of cutoff to the kept message, not to each copy.
followups: A member blocks the recruiter instead of answering. Should that count as a response, and how would you add it without breaking last quarter's numbers?
The admin wants the rate per recruiter, and seats are reassigned when a recruiter leaves. What does the data need, and which recruiter gets a message sent before the transfer?
Members in some regions respond on weekends only. Is a 7-day window fair across regions, and how would you check?
At hundreds of millions of messages a month, how would you compute this daily without rescanning, given a response can arrive up to 7 days later?

rules.ask: A seat messaged the same member twice, a month apart. How many messages does your query count, and how many should it?
How do you decide which copies belong to the same group when they are more than the limit apart from the first but close to each other?
A member read the message within an hour and never answered. Is that a response in your query?
The member replied to the second copy, not the first. Does your join still credit the kept message?
Your cutoff uses the clock. What does the same query return if it is rerun next week, and should it?

templates.title: Skills coverage — how many members list every skill a job requires
templates.subtopic: inverted index as bitsets, set intersection, privacy thresholds on aggregates

sections.scenario: When a company drafts a job posting on a professional network, it sees an estimate of how many members list all of the skills the posting requires, so it can tell whether the requirements are realistic. The estimate is an aggregate count: it never identifies a member, and members who chose not to be included in such insights are left out (this exercise's rule; check current docs). The team needs to compute it for a batch of draft postings against a snapshot of profiles.
sections.problem: Implement skills_coverage(profiles, jobs, opted_out=None, min_count=None). profiles[i] is the list of skills member i lists on their profile (a skill may appear more than once); jobs[j] is the list of skills job j requires. Return a list with one integer per job, in job order: the number of members whose profile lists every required skill. A job with no required skills is matched by every counted member. {{norm_rule}} {{min_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 25 000 members with 3–14 skills each and 1 200 jobs with 1–4 required skills in the timing check, drawn from a vocabulary of a few hundred skills, some far more common than others. Checking every member against every job is tens of millions of subset tests and too slow; aim for work proportional to the skills involved, not to members × jobs.
sections.assumptions: Profiles, skills and jobs are hypothetical. Skills come only from what members chose to list on their profile; nothing is inferred. The result is used only as a count.
sections.criteria: Correct "all skills" semantics with duplicates collapsed on both sides; the empty job and the empty profile right; an inverted index built once, with bitset or set intersection per job (not a scan of members per job); at Hard, consistent normalisation and opted-out members excluded before counting; at Very Hard, the minimum applied to the final count with the -1 sentinel; can discuss memory at scale, threshold queries and differencing risks.

clarifications.q: Does a member need all required skills or any of them?
clarifications.a: All of them.

clarifications.q: A job lists the same skill twice. Does a member need it twice?
clarifications.a: No. Requirements are a set; a repeated skill is one requirement.

clarifications.q: Is a member with no skills counted for a job with no requirements?
clarifications.a: Yes. An empty requirement set is met by every counted member.

clarifications.q: Can I return the matching members as well?
clarifications.a: No. Return counts only.

clarifications.q: Are skill names ever misspelt or synonyms?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; mapping synonyms is a follow-up.

hints: Build an inverted index once: for each skill, the members who list it.
Store each skill's members as a bitset (a Python int with bit i set for member i); a job's count is the popcount of the AND of its skills' bitsets.
Build each bitset with a bytearray and int.from_bytes, or AND the rarest skill first and stop as soon as the result is zero.
followups: The vocabulary grows to 40 000 skills and the members to 900 million. How much memory do dense bitsets need, and what would you use instead?
Hiring teams want "members with at least 3 of these 5 skills". How does your structure change?
Skills have synonyms and a hierarchy ("PostgreSQL" implies "SQL"). Where do you apply the mapping, and how do you keep counts comparable when the taxonomy changes?
Two drafts that differ by one skill could reveal something about a small set of members by subtraction. How would you guard against that beyond a per-query minimum?

rules.ask: How many subset checks does that do for 1 200 jobs and 25 000 members, and how long will it take in CPython?
How do you build each skill's bitset without an O(members) operation for every single member you add?
In which order do you intersect a job's skills, and when can you stop early?
Do you normalise the job's skills the same way as the profiles' skills, and where would a mismatch show up?
Do opted-out members ever enter your index, or do you subtract them at the end? Which is safer?

templates.title: Salary insight medians that appear only once k reports exist
templates.subtopic: running median with two heaps, lazy deletion, minimum-group-size thresholds

sections.scenario: A professional network shows salary insights for a job title in a city, built from salaries members report. A median is shown only once a group has at least k reports, so that no single member's salary can be read off the page (this exercise's rule; check current docs). Reports stream in, and the insight must be current after every one.
sections.problem: Implement salary_medians(events, k, lo=None, hi=None). Each event is ("add", title, city, salary) with an integer salary, or ("remove", i). Reports are grouped by (title, city). After each event, return the median salary of the group the event affects if that group has at least k reports, otherwise None. For an odd count the median is the middle salary; for an even count it is the mean of the two middle salaries rounded half up to a whole number ((a + b + 1) // 2). Return one value per event, in order. {{key_rule}} {{band_rule}} {{remove_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 120 000 events in the timing check, most of them in one large group; k ≥ 1. Sorting a group after every report is quadratic in the group size and too slow; aim for O(log n) per event.
sections.assumptions: Titles, cities, salaries, k and the band are hypothetical. Salaries are positive integers in one currency per year. The output is a group statistic only; individual reports are never returned.
sections.criteria: Correct grouping, None below k, the even-count rounding rule; two heaps kept balanced with O(log n) per event; at Hard, consistent key normalisation and band rejection that leaves the group unchanged; at Very Hard, removals with lazy deletion, live counts used for balancing, and no-op removals of rejected or already removed reports; can discuss percentiles, memory at many groups, and differencing risks.

clarifications.q: What does an event return when its group is below k?
clarifications.a: None, even if other groups have medians.

clarifications.q: How is an even count's median rounded?
clarifications.a: The mean of the two middle salaries, rounded half up: 100 000 and 100 001 give 100 001.

clarifications.q: Are equal salaries separate reports?
clarifications.a: Yes. Two members reporting the same salary are two reports.

clarifications.q: Is "Data Engineer" in Austin the same group as "Data Engineer" in Berlin?
clarifications.a: No. A group is a (title, city) pair.

hints: Keep two heaps per group: a max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half, with the lower half at most one larger.
After every insert, move one element across if the sizes are out of balance; the median is then read from the tops.
For removals, mark the report as gone and keep live counts per heap; discard gone elements only when they reach a top (lazy deletion). Store (salary, index) pairs so equal salaries stay distinct.
followups: The page also shows the 25th and 75th percentiles. How do you extend your structure, and what does each event cost now?
There are 2 million (title, city) groups, most with a handful of reports. What is the memory cost of two heaps per group, and when would you not keep them in memory?
A median of exactly k reports can still reveal something if one report is added or removed between two page views. How would you limit that?
Reports are stored in a warehouse and the insight is recomputed nightly instead. Which SQL would you write, and when is a streaming structure worth it?

rules.ask: How many times does your code sort a 100 000-report group across 120 000 events?
bisect finds the position in O(log n). What does inserting into the middle of a Python list cost, and how does that grow?
Python's heapq is a min-heap. How do you keep the lower half, and how do you break ties between equal salaries?
Removing from the middle of a heap and re-heapifying is O(n). How would you avoid it?
Your heaps contain removed reports. Which counts do you use to balance them, and when are the removed ones actually dropped?

templates.title: Learning path — the fewest courses that teach a target skill set
templates.subtopic: set cover over skill bitmasks, lexicographic cost

sections.scenario: A member opens the learning catalogue and names the skills they want for their next role, say SQL, Airflow, Kafka and data modeling. Each course in the catalogue teaches a few skills and takes a known number of minutes. Members finish short plans and abandon long ones, so the product wants to suggest the plan with the fewest courses, and among plans with the same number of courses, the one with the fewest minutes. The member's goal is the input; nothing is inferred about the member beyond what they typed and what their own profile lists.
sections.problem: Implement learning_path(target, courses, known=None). target is a list of skill names. courses is a list of (course_id, minutes, skills), where skills lists the skills the course teaches, some of which may be outside the target. A plan is a set of courses that together teach every target skill not in known. Return (number_of_courses, total_minutes) for the plan with the fewest courses, and the fewest total minutes among those. Return (0, 0) when nothing is left to learn. {{coverage_rule}} {{known_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 16 skills left to learn and 120 courses. Minutes are positive integers below 1 000. A course teaches at most 8 skills. Something close to O(2ᵏ · n) for k skills and n courses is expected. Trying every combination of courses is not fast enough: the best plan can need six or more courses.
sections.assumptions: The catalogue, its skills and the minutes are hypothetical. Skill names are already standardised, so two spellings of one skill do not occur. A course teaches every skill it lists to the level the member asked for, and the member takes courses in any order.
sections.criteria: Correct (courses, minutes) with the fewest courses first; None when a needed skill is taught nowhere and (0, 0) when nothing is left; known skills and duplicates removed before planning; skills outside the target ignored; a subset DP over the needed skills with one state per mask; duplicate course masks collapsed; integer arithmetic; a clear complexity argument; sensible answers on prerequisites, time budgets and large targets.

clarifications.q: Do I return the course ids?
clarifications.a: No. Return the pair (number_of_courses, total_minutes). It is unique even when several plans tie.

clarifications.q: Does a course that teaches skills outside the target cost anything extra?
clarifications.a: Only its minutes. The extra skills neither help nor hurt.

clarifications.q: Is a plan of two long courses better than a plan of three short ones?
clarifications.a: Yes. Fewer courses first, then fewer minutes.

clarifications.q: Can I take the same course twice?
clarifications.a: Taking it twice never helps, so a plan is a set of courses.

clarifications.q: Can two courses have the same id?
clarifications.a: No. Ids are unique, but two different courses can teach exactly the same skills.

hints: With 16 skills there are 65 536 subsets of skills. Number the skills that are still needed and turn each course into a bitmask.
Let best[mask] be the cheapest way to teach at least the skills in mask. Going from mask through a course reaches mask | course_mask.
Many courses have the same mask; keep only the shortest one per mask. Compare (courses, minutes) as a tuple, or pack the pair into one integer.
followups: Members want to see the plan, not only its size. How do you return the courses, and which plan do you show when several tie?
Some courses require another course first. How does that change the problem, and does the subset DP still work?
The member also has a weekly time budget, and wants the fewest weeks rather than the fewest courses. What is the new objective, and what is the new state?
A member asks for 40 skills, and 2⁴⁰ states are out of reach. What would you do, and how would you tell how far your answer is from the best plan?

rules.ask: Give a target where taking the course that teaches the most missing skills first leads to three courses when two would do.
How many combinations of six courses are there in a catalogue of 80, and how long would your loop take in Python?
How many states does your memo hold for 16 skills, and how many transitions does each state try? Write the total.
Your sentinel is a float next to integer minutes. Where could a float reach the returned pair, and how would you keep it exact?
Hashing a frozenset per state works. What does a bitmask give you instead, and how much faster is it?

templates.title: Former colleagues — overlapping stints at the same company
templates.subtopic: overlap of at least D days, interval shrinking, sorting and binary search

sections.scenario: A member's profile lists positions: a company, a start date and an end date, or no end date for a role they still hold. A page that only the member sees tells them, for each company on their profile, how many other members worked there at the same time as them for at least {{min_days}} days. Short overlaps, such as a week's handover, are not counted. The numbers are computed offline for every member, so they have to be computed for millions of positions in one pass.
sections.problem: Implement former_colleagues(positions, min_days, today, opted_out=None). positions is a list of (member, company, start_day, end_day). Days are integers and both ends are inclusive, so a position from day 10 to day 10 lasts one day. A member's positions at one company form one stint, from the earliest start to the latest end. Two stints at the same company, held by different members, overlap by min(end) − max(start) + 1 days when that is positive. Return a dict {member: {company: n}} with an entry for every member and every company they held a position at, where n is the number of other members whose stint at that company overlapped theirs by at least min_days days (0 if none). An empty input returns {}. {{position_rule}} {{privacy_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 positions. Almost half of them can be at one large company, and many stints there last years. min_days is at least 1. Something close to O(n log n) is expected. Comparing every pair of stints at a company, even after sorting by start, is too slow when thousands of stints are open at the same time.
sections.assumptions: Members, companies and dates are hypothetical. Positions are already linked to one company page each, so renamed or merged companies are not a concern here. Every position starts on or before today, and every ended position ends on or before it. Only positions the member chose to show on their profile are in the input.
sections.criteria: Inclusive day arithmetic with the exact min_days boundary; positions merged into one stint per member and company before counting; current positions running to today; opted-out members neither counted nor listed; every member and company present with 0 where nothing qualifies; stints shorter than min_days handled; an O(n log n) count by shrinking stints and binary search (or an equivalent sweep with a Fenwick tree), justified; output that is the member's own view only; credible answers on names and visibility, returning employees and freshness.

clarifications.q: Is the overlap counted in whole days, both ends included?
clarifications.a: Yes. Two positions from day 1 to day 90 overlap by 90 days.

clarifications.q: A colleague held two positions at the company during my stint. Do they count twice?
clarifications.a: No. Their positions form one stint, and they count once.

clarifications.q: Could two short positions overlap enough together when neither does alone?
clarifications.a: Yes. That is why positions are merged into stints first.

clarifications.q: Does a member count themself?
clarifications.a: Never. Only other members are counted.

clarifications.q: What does today do?
clarifications.a: A position with no end date runs until today, inclusive.

hints: Overlap ≥ D means min(e₁, e₂) − max(s₁, s₂) ≥ D − 1. Write that as four inequalities. Which two hold for any stint of at least D days?
A stint shorter than D days can never qualify. For the others, shrink [s, e] to [s, e − D + 1]. When do two shrunken intervals intersect?
The intervals that intersect [a, b] are those that start at or before b, minus those that end before a. Two sorted arrays and bisect give both counts.
followups: The page should show the colleagues' names, not only the count. Whose visibility settings decide which names may appear, and what do you do for a colleague who hides their connections or their positions?
A member who left a company and came back has two stints there. A colleague who overlapped both should still count once. How does your counting change?
Positions arrive all day as members edit their profiles. How would you keep the counts fresh without recomputing everything?
Positions are given in months, not days, on most profiles. How do you treat "March 2021 to May 2021", and how do you explain the rule to the member?

rules.ask: The largest company has 30 000 stints that last years. How many pairs is that, and how long would it run?
Your sweep stops at the first later start. How many open stints does each step still visit when stints last five years?
Is a tree needed here once every stint is shrunk by D − 1 days, or do two sorted arrays do? Explain which counting problem is left.
How do you merge one member's promotions at a company before counting, and what goes wrong if you do not?
Profiles give months, not days. Which day would you pick for "started in March", and does that choice change who counts?

templates.title: Debug the creator post analytics report
templates.subtopic: reshare attribution, edited posts, deletion, time zones, distinct counts

sections.scenario: Members who post regularly see a daily report on their own posts: views, unique viewers and reactions per post and day. The report is shown only to the creator and holds counts, never a list of viewers. Creators have raised several complaints about one job. An edited post shows up as two posts. Views from members who reshared a post disappear, while a creator who reshared someone else's post sees that post in their report. A member who deleted their account still adds to view counts. Creators in Asia and the Americas see late-evening views on the wrong day. A reader who comes back the next day is never counted as a unique viewer again. The function below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix creator_report(creator, offset_min, posts, events, deleted) so that it meets this specification. {{replay_rule}}

  1. posts maps a post id to {"author", "reshare_of"}. reshare_of is None for an original post. For a reshare it names the original post, which is always an original and always in posts.
  2. events are {"type": "view" | "react", "post", "member", "ts"}, with ts in Unix seconds (UTC). An event's post id may carry an edit suffix, as in p-1041#v2. An edit does not change the post's identity, so the event belongs to p-1041. Events for a post id that is not in posts are ignored.
  3. Attribution. An event on a reshare is credited to the original post. Only events credited to a post whose author is creator are reported.
  4. Exclusions. Events from members in deleted (deleted accounts) are dropped completely: they add to no count. The creator's own events are dropped too.
  5. Day. Each event is counted on the creator's local date: (ts + offset_min · 60) // 86400 days after 1970-01-01, written as YYYY-MM-DD. offset_min is the creator's offset from UTC in minutes, for example 330 for UTC+05:30 and −300 for UTC−05:00.
  6. Output. One row [day, post, views, unique_viewers, reactions] for every local day and credited post with at least one counted event, sorted by day and then post id. views counts view events, unique_viewers counts distinct members who viewed that post on that local day, and reactions counts react events.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's shape and output format. Up to 200 000 events, processed in linear time.
sections.assumptions: Event shapes, ids and offsets are hypothetical and simplified. Each event is delivered once. The creator's offset is fixed for the whole report; daylight-saving changes are out of scope here.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with the creator's symptom; edit suffix stripped before keying rows; reshares credited to the original and authorship checked on the original; deleted accounts excluded from every count; the offset added, not subtracted, with correct dates for negative offsets; unique viewers per post and local day; the creator's own events excluded; minimal, linear fixes; a regression test per bug.

clarifications.q: Do views of a reshare count as views of the original post?
clarifications.a: Yes. They are credited to the original, and its author sees them.

clarifications.q: I reshared someone else's post. Do views of my reshare appear in my report?
clarifications.a: No. They are credited to the original post, which is not yours.

clarifications.q: Should a deleted account's views count in views but not in unique_viewers?
clarifications.a: No. Deletion is honoured everywhere: the events add to no count.

clarifications.q: Is a viewer unique per post, or per post and day?
clarifications.a: Per post and local day. A reader who comes back the next day is unique on both days.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Run one view of p-1#v2 and one of p-1 through the code. How many rows come out?
Whose authorship does the code check for an event on a reshare: the resharer's or the original author's?
Take a creator at UTC+05:30 and a view at 20:00 UTC. What local date and time is that, and what does the code compute?
Follow a deleted member's view through every counter, not only one.
followups: The report runs daily for every creator. How would you compute it for all creators in one pass, and what is the key you aggregate on?
A member deletes their account a month after viewing a post. Which already published daily numbers change, and how do you recompute them?
A creator moves from UTC−08:00 to UTC+01:00. Do past days move, and what would the creator expect to see?
Unique viewers per week cannot be summed from unique viewers per day. How would you report weekly reach without keeping every viewer id for ever?

rules.ask: Post ids are opaque strings. What would your suffix handling do to an id that itself contains the characters you strip?
The report takes a fixed offset. What changes if the creator's time zone has daylight saving time, and which offset applies to an event?
Your set holds viewer ids for each post and day. How large does it grow for a post with millions of views, and what would you use at that scale?
The deletion arrives after yesterday's report was published. What do you recompute, and how do you prove the member's events no longer count?
Could a reshare of a reshare reach this function? What would you change if reshare_of could name another reshare?

templates.title: Job alerts — matching new postings to saved searches
templates.subtopic: stream matching, frequency caps, delivery, measuring outcomes

cap: one push notification a day and one email digest a week

sections.scenario: Members save job searches: keywords, a title, a location or remote, seniority, a company list, and a minimum salary when the posting states one. When a new posting matches a saved search, the member can be alerted by email or push notification. There are about {{saved_searches}} saved searches and {{new_postings}} new postings. Members who receive too many alerts unsubscribe, so each member gets at most {{cap}}, and alerts must say something useful when they do arrive. The jobs team also wants to know whether alerts lead to applications, counting an application within {{attribution_window}} of the alert.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from a posting being published to an alert being delivered, and the measurement that follows. Cover how saved searches are stored and indexed so a posting finds its matching searches without testing all of them; how matches are collected per member and ranked with a scoring function you are given; how frequency caps, quiet hours and the member's notification settings are applied; how a posting that closes or is edited before the alert goes out is handled; deduplication, so a member never hears about the same posting twice; and how you measure applications that follow alerts without counting applications that would have happened anyway.
sections.constraints: A posting closed or removed before delivery must not be alerted. A member's notification settings and unsubscribes apply at send time, not at match time. Alerts must not reveal anything the poster restricted. Retries anywhere in the pipeline must not send an alert twice. Measurement uses aggregates; no report lists individual members' applications.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, caps and windows are hypothetical. The relevance scoring function is given to you as a black box that takes a posting and a saved search and returns a score; you do not design it. Postings are already normalised to a standard title, location and seniority.
sections.criteria: Saved searches indexed so a posting finds candidates without a full scan; matching separated from delivery with per-member queues; caps, quiet hours, settings and unsubscribes enforced at send time; closed or edited postings revalidated before sending; idempotent delivery keyed by member and posting; a holdout or randomised design for measuring applications, reported as aggregates; a plan for bulk postings and hot matches; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Must the alert go out the moment a posting is published?
clarifications.a: Freshness matters, but members also chose a cadence: some want daily digests, others instant pushes. Design for both.

clarifications.q: Can one posting match thousands of searches?
clarifications.a: Yes. A broad title in a large city can match hundreds of thousands of searches. That is the main load problem.

clarifications.q: What if a member has five saved searches that match the same posting?
clarifications.a: They hear about it once.

clarifications.q: How do we know an alert caused an application?
clarifications.a: You do not, from correlation alone. Explain what you would compare against.

clarifications.q: Who sees the measurement?
clarifications.a: The jobs product team, as aggregates by cadence, channel and search type.

hints: Invert the problem: index saved searches by their most selective required field (title, location, company), so a posting looks up a small candidate set and only those are fully checked.
Separate matching from delivery. Matches go into a per-member queue; a scheduler applies caps, quiet hours and settings when it is time to send.
Hold out a small random share of matches from being sent, and compare their application rate with the alerted group's.
followups: A popular title in a large city matches a quarter of all saved searches. Walk through what your matcher and your queues do with that posting.
A posting is edited to raise the salary after matching but before the digest is sent. Which searches does it now match, and what does the digest show?
How do you make "never alert the same posting twice" hold across retries, digests and push notifications?
The alerted group applies at 3 times the rate of non-alerted members. Why is that not the effect of alerts, and what number would you report instead?
At {{saved_searches}} saved searches, half belong to members who have not opened an alert in a year. What would you do, and what would you measure first?

rules.ask: How many comparisons is that per posting at {{saved_searches}} searches, and what index would cut it?
Which field do you index a search under when it has a title, a location and a salary floor, and what is still checked after the lookup?
What is your partition key for the per-member alert queue, and why does it make the frequency cap easy to enforce?
Members who save searches are already looking hard. How do you separate the alert's effect from that, and what is your control group?
Where is the record of "already alerted" stored, keyed by what, and for how long?

incidents: A large employer bulk-publishes 30 000 near-identical postings in ten minutes, and each matches a large share of the {{saved_searches}} saved searches.
A delivery worker crashes after sending a batch of emails but before recording them as sent, and restarts from its last checkpoint.
A posting is closed ten minutes after matching, but it is already queued in thousands of members' pending alerts, and each of those members gets at most {{cap}}.

templates.title: Learning progress from many devices
templates.subtopic: offline sync, merging progress, completions, employer reporting with privacy limits

devices: a phone, a tablet and a laptop, often offline on the phone
completion_rule: watched at least 90% of every video and passed the quiz
watched every video to the end and passed the final assessment

sections.scenario: Learners watch course videos on {{devices}}. The player reports progress as it plays, and the phone keeps watching offline and uploads later. A course is complete when the learner has {{completion_rule}}, and a completion earns a certificate the learner can add to their profile. There are about {{learners}} active learners. Some learn through an employer licence with up to {{employer_seats}} seats, and the employer's learning admin sees progress reports for learning done under that licence.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline from the player's progress events to three outputs: the learner's own "continue where you left off" and progress view, completions and certificates, and the employer admin's reports. Cover the event format and what makes an upload safe to retry; how progress from several devices, uploaded late and out of order, is merged into one state per learner and video; when a course becomes complete and how a certificate is issued exactly once; what the employer admin may see and what they may not; and how a learner's deletion request or the end of an employer licence is honoured in every output.
sections.constraints: Offline uploads can be days late. Progress must never go backwards because an old device uploads late. A certificate, once issued, is not revoked by a late or duplicate event. Employer reports cover only learning done under that employer's licence, and only what the licence terms allow. A deleted learner disappears from every report.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, rules and terms are hypothetical; check current product documentation for real rules. Each device has a stable id and a clock that can be wrong by minutes or hours. The player can report the set of seconds watched, not just a position.
sections.criteria: Idempotent, retry-safe uploads with event and upload times kept separately; watched progress as a union of intervals merged in any order; resume position chosen by event time; completion evaluated from merged state with certificates issued exactly once; licence context attached at ingestion and employer reports limited to it and its terms; deletion and licence end honoured in every output; a plan for compacting interval state at scale; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: Is progress the furthest position reached?
clarifications.a: No. A learner who skips to the end has not watched the video. Progress is the share of the video actually watched, across all devices.

clarifications.q: Which device's position is used to resume?
clarifications.a: The most recent session, by the time it happened, not the time it uploaded.

clarifications.q: Can the employer admin see courses the learner took on their own, outside the licence?
clarifications.a: No. Only learning under the licence.

clarifications.q: What does the admin see after a learner leaves the employer?
clarifications.a: Aggregates for the licence period may remain; the learner's identity in reports follows the licence terms and deletion requests.

clarifications.q: Do quiz answers go to the employer?
clarifications.a: Only pass or fail and the date, if the licence terms say so.

hints: Make progress a merge of watched intervals per learner and video: a union is commutative and idempotent, so late and duplicate uploads are harmless.
Keep "resume position" separate from "watched": the first is the latest session by event time, the second is the union of intervals.
Tag every event with the licence it happened under at ingestion, so employer reports never have to guess.
followups: The phone uploads three days of offline viewing after the laptop has already moved on. Walk through what the learner sees on each device.
A completion is computed, the certificate is issued, and then a correction shows that one video was below the threshold. What do you do, and what do you tell the learner?
An employer wants a report of who has not started a required course. What can that report show, and what must it never show?
A learner asks for their data to be deleted. Which stores, aggregates and certificates change, and how do you show it was done?
At {{learners}} learners, the union of watched intervals per video is too large to rewrite on every event. How do you store and compact it?

rules.ask: An old phone uploads a position from three days ago. What does last-write-wins by upload time do to resume, and what does max-position do to completion?
Your merge is idempotent. Is resume position also safe to merge in any order, and which timestamp decides it?
A device clock is two hours fast. Which outputs does that affect, and how do you bound the damage?
A learner took a personal-interest course on the same account. Which field keeps it out of the employer's report, and where is it set?
Two completion jobs run at once for the same learner after a retry. What stops two certificates?

incidents: A mobile release holds offline progress for a week. After the next update, catch-up uploads from a large share of the {{learners}} learners arrive within one day, most of them out of order.
An employer licence with {{employer_seats}} seats ends at midnight, and the admin exports a report at 00:05.
A bug double-counted watched seconds for one day, and 4% of learners were marked complete for courses they had not finished.

templates.title: Member profile history — what a profile said on a date, with edits and deletions honoured
templates.subtopic: bitemporal profile entries, valid time versus recorded time, erasure in versioned stores

sections.scenario: A professional network holds about {{members}} member profiles. A profile has a headline, a location, positions (title, a linked company page or free-text company name, start and end month, description), education entries and skills. Members make about {{daily_edits}} edits a day: they add a position that started years ago, correct a start month, change a title, delete an entry, hide a section, or close their account. Several readers need the profile at a point in time: the member's own "edit history" page, job-application records that keep the profile as it was submitted, a matching model that is trained elsewhere and needs features as of each application date (a scoring function you are given; this design only supplies point-in-time inputs), and aggregate reports such as "members listing a skill, by region and month". In this exercise's policy (check current docs for any real product), prior versions of an edited entry are kept for {{history_days}} days; a deleted entry, or every entry of a closed account, is removed from every store, including derived tables, within {{erase_days}} days.
sections.problem: Design the data model for profile history. Cover: the member and each kind of profile entry, with stable entry ids that survive edits; how versions are stored so that two different questions can both be answered — "what did this profile say at time T" (recorded time) and "where did this member work in month M, as we know it now" (valid time); section visibility and how readers respect it; what an application stores so the employer sees exactly what was submitted; how point-in-time features are produced without leaking later edits; and how a deletion or account closure removes every version within {{erase_days}} days from the versioned store, snapshots, derived tables and caches. Define the tables and grains for "members listing skill S by region and month" and say which published numbers change after a deletion.
sections.constraints: An edit never overwrites: prior versions are kept for {{history_days}} days. Readers other than the member see only sections visible to them under the member's settings at the time of reading. Erasure within {{erase_days}} days is complete, including derived copies. Aggregate reports publish a cell only when it covers at least a minimum number of members. No protected trait (age, gender, ethnicity, health, religion, disability) is inferred from profile content, for any reader.
sections.assumptions: Member counts, edit rates and both retention periods are hypothetical, and the policy is this exercise's own. Positions carry month precision; edits carry a server timestamp. An application is a separate product record that the member chose to send; what it keeps is part of that record, under its own retention rule.
sections.criteria: Entry-level versions with stable ids; valid time and recorded time kept separate and used correctly in the two example questions; visibility applied at read time; application copies kept as part of the application record; point-in-time features filtered on recorded time; an erasure path that reaches snapshots, derived tables and caches within {{erase_days}} days (per-member keys, delete vectors or crypto-shredding); aggregate grain, minimum-member threshold and restatement policy stated; no inferred protected traits; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Can a member add a position that started before they joined the network?
clarifications.a: Yes. Valid time (when the job was held) is often years before recorded time (when the entry was written).

clarifications.q: What does deleting an entry mean for its history?
clarifications.a: Every version of that entry disappears from every store within {{erase_days}} days, including its past versions in the edit history. Hiding a section is different: the data stays, readers stop seeing it.

clarifications.q: Does an application keep the profile the member sent?
clarifications.a: Yes, as part of the application record, and the employer sees that copy. It follows the application's retention, not the profile's.

clarifications.q: Do aggregate reports already published need to be recomputed after a deletion?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, published cells that met the minimum-member threshold stay as published; every later computation excludes the deleted data.

clarifications.q: Can two edits of the same entry arrive out of order?
clarifications.a: Yes. Mobile clients retry, so an older edit can arrive after a newer one.

hints: Give every entry its own id and store versions of it, not versions of the whole profile.
Each version needs two time ranges: when it was true (start and end month) and when the system held it (recorded_from, recorded_to).
Erasure is easiest when every derived store is keyed so that "all rows of this entry or member" can be found and removed, or made unreadable, in one step.
followups: Show the version rows for one position: added today with a start month three years ago, title corrected next week, then deleted. What does each reader see before and after the deletion?
The matching model needs features "as of each application date". Write the shape of the point-in-time join, and say which time range it filters on.
Your history lives in immutable columnar files. How do you erase one member's entries within {{erase_days}} days without rewriting the whole table every day?
"Members listing skill S by region and month": define the grain and say what happens to next month's number and to last month's published number when 2% of those members delete the skill.
At {{daily_edits}} edits a day, compare entry versions with a daily full-profile snapshot on storage, on point-in-time reads and on erasure cost.

rules.ask: At {{members}} profiles, how many copies of an unchanged headline does a daily snapshot keep in {{history_days}} days, and how many files must you rewrite to erase one member?
Is valid_from the start month of the job or the moment the member typed it? A member adds a 2019 position today: what does "profile as of last month" return?
The flag is set, but who can still read the row, in which copies, and on which day is it actually gone?
How do you answer "members who added skill S in month M" without parsing every version of every profile?
An older edit arrives after a newer one because the phone retried. Which timestamp orders the versions, and what does the member's edit history show?

incidents: A member closed their account, and {{erase_days}} days later their former headline still appears in a point-in-time training extract: the extract was materialised from a monthly snapshot the erasure job did not know about.

A bulk import from a résumé upload wrote every position with the upload month as its start month; "positions started this month" jumped tenfold and a hiring-trends chart went out before anyone noticed.

Retried edits from a mobile client arrived out of order, and ordering versions by arrival time made an old title current again for thousands of members, some of whom had applied to jobs with the wrong title shown.

templates.title: Job postings and applications — reposts, closures, status changes and what the applicant is shown
templates.subtopic: posting identity across reposts, application status history, employer stages mapped to applicant-visible states

sections.scenario: Employers publish about {{daily_postings}} job postings a day on a professional network, some typed in directly and about {{ats_share}} sent from employers' applicant tracking systems through a feed. A posting can be edited (title, location, workplace type, salary range), closed by the poster, closed automatically after {{auto_close_days}} days, reopened, or reposted as a new posting for the same opening. Members submit about {{daily_applications}} applications a day: either on the platform, where the application and its later status are recorded, or on the employer's own site, where the platform only knows that the member clicked through. Employers move on-platform applicants through their own pipeline stages, which differ by employer. The applicant sees a short list of statuses — submitted, viewed by the employer, no longer accepting applications, not selected — and in this exercise's rule an applicant is shown "not selected" only when the employer chose to send that status.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: postings and their versions (what the posting said when each member applied); an opening identity that links reposts of the same role, and how it is assigned when the employer provides a requisition id and when it does not; closures and reopenings; applications and their status history; the mapping from each employer's stages to the applicant-visible statuses, and a record of what the applicant was actually shown and when; off-site click-throughs kept separate from applications. Define facts for "applications per posting and day", "time from application to first employer view", "share of applicants who received any status after submission" and "openings reposted more than twice in 90 days".
sections.constraints: Status history is append-only. An applicant never sees an employer's internal stage name, notes or ranking. Salary ranges are shown as the posting stated them at the time of applying. Off-site click-throughs are never counted as applications. A closed posting accepts no new applications, and its existing applications keep their history.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares and the auto-close period are hypothetical. Employer pipeline stages are configured per employer and can change. The visible statuses and the "not selected" rule are this exercise's; check current docs for any real product.
sections.criteria: Opening, posting and posting version as distinct identities with a stated repost rule and its error measurement; applications tied to the version applied against; append-only status history; employer stages and visible statuses as separate, versioned mappings; what the applicant was shown recorded as its own event; off-site clicks never counted as applications; closure reasons recorded; facts at stated grains with a finality rule; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Is a repost the same posting?
clarifications.a: No, it gets a new posting id. Whether it is the same opening is what your model must decide, from a requisition id if the employer sends one or from evidence such as company, title, location and timing.

clarifications.q: What happens to applications when a posting closes?
clarifications.a: They keep their status history; the applicant is shown "no longer accepting applications" for the posting, and their own application status continues if the employer keeps working on it.

clarifications.q: Can the salary range change after people have applied?
clarifications.a: Yes. Each application must point to the posting version it was submitted against.

clarifications.q: For off-site applies, do we know if the member applied?
clarifications.a: No. We know they clicked through. Nothing more is inferred.

clarifications.q: Can an employer move an applicant backwards in their pipeline?
clarifications.a: Yes, and stages can be renamed or removed by the employer at any time.

hints: Separate three identities: the opening (the role the employer is filling), the posting (one publication of it), and the posting version (what it said between two edits).
Keep employer stages and applicant-visible statuses as two histories joined by a mapping that is itself versioned.
Record what was shown to the applicant as its own event, not as something recomputed from the current mapping.
followups: Show the rows for one opening: posted, salary range edited after 40 applications, auto-closed after {{auto_close_days}} days, reposted with a new id, then filled. What does each applicant see?
Without a requisition id, how do you decide two postings are the same opening, and how do you measure how often that decision is wrong?
An employer renames a stage and maps it to a different visible status. What happens to applicants already in that stage, and to last month's "received any status" metric?
"Time from application to first employer view" for applications that were never viewed: what do you report, and when is a month's number final?
At {{daily_applications}} applications a day, which tables are append-only facts, which are accumulating snapshots, and how is "what was shown" reproducible a year later?

rules.ask: The same role is closed after {{auto_close_days}} days and reposted with a new id. How does your model count it — two jobs, or one opening posted twice — and which number do job seekers care about?
An applicant went from viewed to interviewing and back to viewed. With one status column, what was the applicant shown last Tuesday?
How do you keep off-site clicks out of "applications", and what may you claim about whether those members applied?
The range was raised after 40 people applied. Which range does each application record show, and what does the employer report compare?
Two employers both have a stage called "Screen" meaning different things. How do your reports compare them, and what does the applicant see?

incidents: An employer's tracking system was migrated and re-sent every open posting with new ids; overnight about {{ats_share}} of that day's postings looked new, and applications attached to the old ids looked orphaned to applicants.
A stage mapping for one large employer sent "not selected" to thousands of applicants whose applications had only been auto-sorted, not reviewed; support tickets arrived within an hour.

Postings auto-closed after {{auto_close_days}} days were counted as "filled" in a hiring report because closure reason was not recorded, so time-to-fill fell sharply for employers who simply never closed postings themselves.

templates.title: Company pages and affiliation — acquisitions, rebrands and page merges
templates.subtopic: entity identity over time, merge maps, as-was versus as-is reporting, aggregate privacy floors

sections.scenario: A professional network hosts about {{pages}} company pages. Members link each position on their profile to a page, or type a company name that matches no page. Pages change: a company rebrands (new name, logo and handle on the same page), acquires another company (the acquired page is kept as an affiliated page, or retired into the acquirer's), or duplicate pages created by different people are merged after the owner verifies them — about {{merges_per_month}} merges a month, a few of them later found to be mistakes and undone. Page administrators see aggregate insights: followers over time, employee counts by function and location, and headcount growth. In this exercise's rule, no insight cell is shown for fewer than {{insights_floor}} members, and no insight ever names or lists individual employees.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: organisation and page identity over time (names, handles, rebrands); the merge map, including chains of merges and an unmerge; affiliation between pages (subsidiary, acquired) with effective dates; how a member's position stays linked to the right page through rebrands, merges and acquisitions without editing the member's profile history; free-text companies that are linked to a page later. Define headcount and employee-by-function facts and say whether a page's growth chart shows organisations "as they were" or "as they are now" after a merge or acquisition. Explain how the {{insights_floor}}-member floor is enforced so that a merge, an unmerge or a week-over-week difference cannot reveal a group smaller than the floor.
sections.constraints: A page id, once issued, always resolves: to itself or, after a merge, to the surviving page. An unmerge must restore both pages' followers and position links as they were. Members' positions keep the page they chose; resolution happens at read time. Insight cells below {{insights_floor}} members are suppressed. Insights are aggregates only, about members who list a current or past position at the page.
sections.assumptions: Page counts, merge rates and the floor are hypothetical, and the merge, affiliation and floor rules are this exercise's own. Function and location come from what members list on their profile; nothing is inferred about a member beyond what they listed.
sections.criteria: Organisation, page and merge map with effective times; resolution at read time with chains, cycles and unmerges handled; positions never rewritten; affiliation and acquisition modelled with dates; a stated as-was versus as-is choice for growth charts; free-text linking with evidence and review; the floor enforced on cells and on differences (stable rounding, minimum change, or noise, with the trade-off stated); efficient resolution at warehouse scale (a materialised closure table); each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: After a merge, what happens to the retired page id?
clarifications.a: It resolves to the surviving page. Old links, followers and position links follow it.

clarifications.q: Does an acquisition merge the pages?
clarifications.a: Not necessarily. The acquirer chooses: keep the acquired page as an affiliate, or retire it into the acquirer's page later.

clarifications.q: Should a member who left the acquired company before the acquisition count as the acquirer's alumni?
clarifications.a: Your choice; define it and say what each choice does to the acquirer's insights.

clarifications.q: Can a merge be undone?
clarifications.a: Yes, and the two pages must come back with their own followers and links.

clarifications.q: Can a page administrator see who the employees are?
clarifications.a: Not through insights. Insights are aggregate counts only.

hints: Store the merge map as rows with effective times (from page, into page, merged_at, unmerged_at), and resolve a page id by following it, not by rewriting positions.
Keep "the organisation" and "the page" apart if one organisation can have several pages over time.
The privacy floor must hold for every published cell and for any difference between published cells.
followups: Page A was merged into B, then B into C, then A was found to be a different company and unmerged. Show the merge-map rows and how a position linked to A resolves at each step.
Company C acquires D. Draw C's headcount growth chart for the year before and after, "as was" and "as is". Which does an administrator see, and how is the change labelled?

A function with 52 members at a page drops to 48 after an unmerge. With a floor of {{insights_floor}}, what may be shown, and how do you stop someone subtracting two published numbers to learn about a small group?
Free-text company names: how do you link "Acme Inc." typed by thousands of members to a page later, and what does that do to past headcount numbers?
With about {{merges_per_month}} merges a month, how do you resolve page ids in a warehouse join over billions of positions without following chains row by row?

rules.ask: You rewrote positions from A to B at merge time. The merge is undone a week later: which positions go back to A, and how do you know?
A into B, B into C, and later C into A by mistake. How does your resolution avoid a cycle, and what does a position on A resolve to?
Which members count: current position only, or anyone with a position at any time? And what does an acquisition do to the line on the chart?
Both last week's and this week's cells are above the floor, but their difference is 3. What does a page administrator learn from the two, and how do you prevent it?
Two different companies share a name in different countries. What evidence besides the name do you use, and who confirms a link before it changes counts?

incidents: A duplicate page was merged into the main page and the "employees by function" table, compared week over week, revealed a function group of fewer than {{insights_floor}} people by difference, even though every published cell met the floor.
A rebrand was entered as a new page instead of a rename. Members' positions split across both pages, and the company's headcount chart showed a 40% drop in one month.

A bad merge joined two unrelated companies with the same name. It was undone two weeks later, but followers who had followed the merged page during those weeks could not be assigned back to either page.

templates.title: Recruiter projects — saved candidates, pipeline stages, messages and seat transfers
templates.subtopic: customer-owned work, seat assignment history, stage events with versioned stage definitions, retention

sections.scenario: Companies buy a recruiting product with a number of seats, about {{seats}} seats across all customers here. A seat is assigned to a recruiter. Recruiters create projects (usually one per opening), save member profiles found in search to a project, move candidates through the customer's own pipeline of {{custom_stages}} stages, add notes, and message candidates; the candidate sees the message thread in their own inbox and can reply, decline or ignore it. When a recruiter leaves, the customer's administrator reassigns the seat or transfers that recruiter's projects, notes and threads to a colleague, typically {{transfer_lag_days}} days later. When a contract ends, this exercise's rule keeps the customer's projects, notes and pipeline data for {{retention_days}} days and then deletes them. A candidate can close their account at any time.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: customer, contract, seat, recruiter and the history of who held each seat; projects and who owns them over time; a candidate's membership of a project and their stage history; stage definitions per customer that are renamed, reordered and retired, and how reports stay comparable; notes; message threads shared between a recruiter and a candidate, including what happens to an open thread when the seat changes hands; and what is deleted when the contract ends or the candidate closes their account. Define facts for "candidates reaching each stage per project", "time in stage", "replies to first messages per seat" and "hires per recruiter", and say who gets credit for work done before a transfer.
sections.constraints: Projects, notes and pipeline data belong to the customer, not to the individual recruiter. Stage history is append-only. The candidate sees only the message thread, never notes, stages or other projects. A candidate's profile is shown as the candidate currently shows it, never a saved copy. Contract-end deletion runs {{retention_days}} days after the end date and covers derived tables.
sections.assumptions: Seat counts, stage counts, lags and retention are hypothetical; the ownership, transfer and retention rules are this exercise's own. A candidate can be saved to several projects of the same customer, and to projects of different customers who never see each other's data.
sections.criteria: Customer, contract, seat and seat-assignment history with work owned by the customer; attribution by the seat holder at event time; append-only stage events with versioned stage definitions mapped to a canonical set; profile references, never copies; threads modelled with per-message senders and a transfer rule; contract keys on every customer row and a deletion path that covers derived tables; candidate account closure handled; strict separation between customers; each incident contained, corrected and guarded.

clarifications.q: Who owns a project when its recruiter leaves?
clarifications.a: The customer. Until the administrator transfers it, it stays with the vacated seat and can be read by administrators.

clarifications.q: Does the candidate see the new recruiter after a transfer?
clarifications.a: In this exercise the thread moves to the new seat holder, and the candidate sees the new name on future messages; earlier messages keep the sender who wrote them.

clarifications.q: Can stages change in the middle of a hiring cycle?
clarifications.a: Yes: renamed, reordered, split or retired. Candidates in a retired stage are moved by the administrator.

clarifications.q: Can two customers see that both saved the same candidate?
clarifications.a: Never. Each customer's projects are separate.

clarifications.q: What happens when a candidate closes their account?
clarifications.a: Their profile disappears from every project. Whether the customer's notes about them stay until contract-end deletion is a policy question; say what you would do and why.

hints: Make the seat, not the person, the owner key of work, and keep a seat-assignment history so every action can be attributed to whoever held the seat at the time.
Keep a canonical stage set per customer (or a global one) and map each customer's stage versions to it; record stage changes as events with the stage version in force.
Keep references to member profiles, never copies, and give every customer-owned row a contract key so deletion can find it.
followups: Show the rows for one candidate: saved to a project, messaged, replied, moved through three stages, the recruiter leaves, the seat is transferred {{transfer_lag_days}} days later, the new recruiter marks the hire. Who gets credit for what?
The customer renames and reorders its {{custom_stages}} stages mid-quarter. How do "candidates reaching each stage" and "time in stage" stay comparable across the change?
Replies arrive in an open thread during the {{transfer_lag_days}} days before the transfer. Who sees them, and how is "replies per seat" attributed?
The contract ends. List what is deleted after {{retention_days}} days, what is never deleted early, and what aggregate figures survive.
Three recruiters at the same customer saved the same candidate to three projects. How do you show "already contacted by a colleague" without letting a different customer learn anything?

rules.ask: The recruiter who owns those projects leaves today. With the recruiter as owner, who can open the projects tomorrow, and who is credited with last month's hires?
How long did this candidate spend in each stage, and what was the pipeline on the first of last month?
The candidate hid a position yesterday. What does your saved copy show the recruiter, and how is it erased if they close their account?
The customer renamed "Phone screen" to "Recruiter call" and split it in two. How does a report spanning both versions read?
Which tables, files and caches does contract-end deletion touch, and how do you prove a customer's data is gone after {{retention_days}} days?

incidents: After a batch of seat transfers, the "hires per recruiter" report credited every hire of the departed recruiters to the new seat holders, because attribution read the seat's current holder instead of the holder at the time of each stage change.
A customer reordered its {{custom_stages}} stages so that "Offer" now sorted before "Onsite"; the stage-conversion chart reversed overnight and an administrator escalated a "broken pipeline".

A contract ended, and {{retention_days}} days later the deletion job removed projects and notes but missed a per-customer export table that fed a scheduled report; the report kept arriving with former candidates' names.

templates.title: Profile viewers per week — named and private viewers on the member's own page
templates.subtopic: setting in force at event time, distinct viewers per local week, precedence between modes, closed accounts

sections.scenario: A professional network shows each member who looked at their profile. In this exercise a viewer browses in one of two modes: in named mode they are shown with their name, and in private mode they appear only as an anonymous private viewer. A member can switch mode at any time; every switch is a row in visibility_settings, and the mode in force at the moment of a view is what applies to that view. The weekly summary on a member's own "who viewed your profile" page shows how many distinct people viewed them each week, and how many of those were named and how many private. Only the member sees these numbers. A member who closes their account has their activity removed, so their views disappear from everyone's summaries. The sample has {{members}} members and {{views}} views.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns member_id, week_start, viewers, named_viewers, private_viewers: one row per (viewed member, week) with at least one counted viewer, for the weeks whose start is between {{week_from}} and {{week_to}} inclusive, ordered by member_id, week_start. A week runs from Monday 00:00 to the end of Sunday in the viewed member's own time zone (members.time_zone), and week_start is the date of that local Monday. {{zone_rule}} A view is counted unless the viewer is the viewed member, or the viewer's account is closed (closed_at is not null, whenever it was closed). A view's mode is the viewer's setting in force at viewed_at: the row with the latest effective_at at or before viewed_at; with no such row the viewer is in the default mode, named. Each viewer counts once per (member, week): as named if at least one of their counted views that week was named, otherwise as private. viewers is the number of distinct counted viewers, so it equals named_viewers + private_viewers.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The setting boundary is inclusive: a switch at exactly viewed_at governs that view. Weeks with no counted viewer produce no row. The sample has {{views}} views; production has billions of views a week and members in every time zone.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, members, settings and views. The two modes and their counting rule are this exercise's; check current docs for any real product. The report is the member's own page; nothing here is shown to anyone else, and no viewer attribute other than the mode is used.
sections.criteria: The setting in force at viewed_at chosen exactly (inclusive boundary) with the named default; self-views and closed accounts excluded; one row per (member, week, viewer) before counting; the named-wins rule applied so the two columns add up to viewers; weeks taken in the viewed member's zone and the window applied to local week starts, including the last week; deterministic ordering; can discuss precomputation with closures, time-zone changes and small-count disclosure.

clarifications.q: A viewer looked in private mode on Monday and in named mode on Friday. How do they count?
clarifications.a: Once, as a named viewer. The member was already shown their name that week.

clarifications.q: Which time zone decides the week, the viewer's or the member's?
clarifications.a: The viewed member's: it is their page.

clarifications.q: A viewer switched to private at exactly the second of a view. Which mode applies?
clarifications.a: Private. The latest setting at or before viewed_at is in force.

clarifications.q: A viewer closed their account after the week ended. Do their old views still count?
