clarifications.a: No. A closed account's views are removed from every week.

clarifications.q: A viewer who has never changed their setting?
clarifications.a: They are in the default mode, named.

hints: First attach the mode in force to every view: a correlated subquery (or LATERAL) with ORDER BY effective_at DESC LIMIT 1, wrapped in COALESCE(…, 'named').
Then collapse to one row per (member, week, viewer) with bool_or(mode = 'named') before counting.
Convert before truncating: date_trunc('week', viewed_at AT TIME ZONE time_zone)::date.
followups: At billions of views a week, what would you precompute, and how does a viewer's account closure change numbers you already stored?
A member changes their own time zone. Do past weeks re-bucket, and what does the member expect to see?
A member has exactly one private viewer this week and knows only one person was likely to look. Is the private count itself a disclosure, and what would you change?
After a release, the summary used each viewer's current setting for past views. Who could be harmed, and how fast must it be rolled back?

rules.ask: A viewer switched mode four times. How many rows does one of their views produce in your join, and how do you keep only the setting in force at viewed_at?
Is that the latest setting overall, or the latest at or before the view? A viewer browsed privately last month and switched to named today: what does your query show for last month?
A viewer looked three times in one week. What does your count say, and what should it say?
In which time zone is the timestamp when you truncate it? A view at 02:00 UTC on a Monday of a member in Los Angeles: which week is it?
Which views disappear when a viewer has no setting yet, and should they?

incidents: After a release, past views were labelled with each viewer's current setting. Viewers who had browsed privately and later switched to named suddenly appeared by name on other members' pages for weeks they had chosen to be private.
A viewer closed their account, but precomputed weekly summaries still counted them until a full rebuild a week later; the member saw a named viewer whose profile link no longer opened.
Weeks were bucketed in UTC, so members far east of UTC saw Monday-morning views in the previous week and their "this week" number started low every Monday.

templates.title: Job search freshness: new postings searchable in minutes, closures gone, location, remote and salary filters
templates.subtopic: incremental index updates, deletes, filters, freshness measurement

sections.scenario: A professional network's job search lets members search open postings by keywords, title, company, location (a city or region, with a distance radius), workplace type (on-site, hybrid or remote), seniority and pay, when the employer states a pay range. About {{postings}} postings are open at any time and about {{new_daily}} new ones are published each day. Postings come from a posting form that employers fill in and from {{feeds}} employer feeds that send either full files of their open jobs or changes since the last file. Employers edit postings, close them when the role is filled, and repost them. Results are ordered by a scoring function you are given, owned by another team; it scores a few thousand candidate postings per query, and you treat it as a black box.
sections.problem: Design the path from a posting being published, edited or closed to what a member sees in search. Cover the source of truth for each posting, normalisation (locations to places with coordinates, pay to a comparable annual range, remote eligibility), duplicates of one job arriving from several sources, the index and how it is updated incrementally and rebuilt in full, how closures and edits reach every copy of the index, how the filters are evaluated, the "posted N days ago" label, and how you measure freshness end to end.
sections.constraints: A new posting must be searchable within {{freshness}} of being published (p95), and a closed posting must leave results within the same time. A member must never be able to submit an application to a closed posting, even from a stale results page. Search p99 under 300 ms including the scoring function. A full rebuild of the index takes several hours, so it cannot be the only way changes arrive. The index is served from several regions.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, timings and counts are hypothetical. The posting service is the transactional source of truth for each posting's content and status and emits a change event on every write. This exercise's rules for remote postings: each one names the countries where the employer can hire, and it is shown only to searches for those countries.
sections.criteria: Posting store as the source of truth with a versioned change stream; normalisation of places, pay and remote eligibility as explicit, versioned steps; duplicate detection with a stated key and canonical copy; incremental indexing with ordering by version, tombstones for closures and a fast path for them; rebuilds that converge with the stream before swap; apply-time checks against the source of truth; filter semantics (multiple locations, missing pay) chosen and visible to members; an honest "posted" label for reposts and edits; end-to-end freshness measured per posting and per region; guards on feed files that shrink suddenly; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does a repost count as a new posting for the "posted" label?
clarifications.a: Your call; members distrust old jobs presented as new, and employers want reposts to be seen. Say what the label shows and why.

clarifications.q: How should a pay filter treat hourly pay or another currency?
clarifications.a: Normalise to an annual range in the searcher's currency with a dated exchange rate and a stated hours-per-year assumption; say what the member is shown.

clarifications.q: Do postings with no stated pay appear when a pay filter is set?
clarifications.a: A product decision you should make explicitly; either way, say how the member can tell.

clarifications.q: What does it mean when a full feed file no longer contains a posting?
clarifications.a: Usually that the job closed, but feeds sometimes send partial files by mistake.

clarifications.q: How many locations can one posting have?
clarifications.a: Several office cities, plus remote eligibility in some countries.

hints: Keep the index a projection of the posting store: a change stream keyed by posting id, with a version number on every change, so an older update can never overwrite a newer one.
A full rebuild and the incremental stream must converge: build from a snapshot taken at a known stream position, then replay from that position before the new index takes traffic.
Closures are the change that hurts most when late. Treat them as first-class: a fast path, tombstones, and a final check against the source of truth at apply time.
followups: Walk one posting from "publish" to its first appearance in results. Where is the time spent, and how do you measure each step for every posting, not just a sample?
One employer feed sends a file that is missing 40% of its usual postings. Do you close them? What rule decides?
A member searches for remote roles paying at least a stated amount. How is each filter evaluated, and which postings with no stated pay or multiple locations appear?
The nightly full rebuild runs while updates keep flowing. How do you swap indexes without losing or reordering an update made during the rebuild?
One region's index replica lags 20 minutes behind the others. What do members there see, how do you find out, and what do you do automatically?

rules.ask: A posting is published one minute after the rebuild's snapshot. Walk me through how it reaches the new index before that index takes traffic.
An employer closes a posting at 10:00; a results page cached at 09:58 still lists it. Who sees it, until when, and what happens when they press apply?
A posting names three office cities and remote eligibility in two countries. How many index entries is that, and how does a 50 km radius search treat it?
The same job arrives from the employer's own feed and from a staffing agency's feed with a slightly different title. What is your key, and which copy do members see?
Two updates for one posting reach the indexer out of order. What stops the older one from winning?

incidents: One of the {{feeds}} employer feeds sends a partial file. The pipeline closes 120,000 of that employer's postings; members who saved them see "no longer accepting applications" and the employer's hiring team escalates within the hour.

A large employer bulk-edits 300,000 postings at 09:00. The update stream backs up, indexing lag passes {{freshness}} for three hours, and closures queue behind the edits: members keep finding closed jobs and pressing apply.
A pipeline change treats every edit as a new posting. Jobs open for months show "posted 1 hour ago", and members report the same roles reappearing as new every day.
The exchange-rate table used for pay normalisation stops updating for nine days. Pay filters in one currency now exclude postings whose stated ranges overlap the member's filter.

templates.title: Invitation abuse: invitation limits, mass-invite detection from aggregates, warnings and appeals
templates.subtopic: rate limits, aggregate abuse signals, enforcement ladders, appeals

sections.scenario: Members of a professional network send connection invitations, optionally with a short note. A recipient can accept, ignore, or say they do not know the sender, and can report the invitation; a sender can withdraw a pending one. About {{invites_daily}} invitations are sent each day and about {{new_accounts}} accounts are created each day. Some senders abuse invitations: fake accounts that harvest connections to reach members' networks, mass outreach that recipients find unwelcome, and harassment of one member through repeated invitations. Most heavy senders are legitimate: recruiters, people who just met many others at an event, new members building their network. Under this exercise's rule every member has a weekly invitation limit of {{weekly_limit}}, which may be lowered for an account that shows abuse.
sections.problem: Design the invitation limits and the abuse detection behind them. Cover how the limit is enforced on the send path, which aggregate signals describe a sender's behaviour, how they are computed and how fresh they are, how a score or rule set turns them into actions (a warning, a lower limit, a temporary restriction, a review), what the member is told, how appeals work with {{reviewers}} reviewers, how you protect a single recipient from repeated invitations, and how you measure false positives.
sections.constraints: Detection uses counts and outcomes of invitations (sent, accepted, ignored, marked "don't know", reported, withdrawn), account signals such as age and verification, and security signals such as many accounts created from one network; it never reads private messages, and it never uses or infers protected traits. A send decision adds at most 20 ms. Every enforcement action must be explainable to the member in plain terms and reversible on appeal. The weekly limit must hold even when a sender uses several devices at once.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, limits and staffing are hypothetical, and the weekly limit is this exercise's rule (check current product documentation for real limits). The scoring of abuse is yours to design; nothing here describes any company's real detection.
sections.criteria: Exact per-sender limits on the send path with a stated failure mode; aggregate signals with defined windows, denominators and handling of pending invitations, smoothed for low counts; cross-account detection with care for shared networks; an enforcement ladder from warning to review with plain explanations and appeals; protection for a targeted recipient; no private-message content and no protected traits; false positives measured through appeals and sampled review; monitoring for shifts caused by product changes rather than behaviour; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the weekly limit a calendar week or rolling?
clarifications.a: Your choice; say what the member sees when they reach it and when it resets.

clarifications.q: An ignored invitation never gets an answer. When does it count against the sender?
clarifications.a: Invitations can stay pending for weeks. Decide how a signal treats pending ones and say why.

clarifications.q: Can a restriction be automatic?
clarifications.a: Warnings and lower limits can be. A restriction that blocks invitations needs either a high-confidence rule or a review, and always an appeal.

clarifications.q: Are some members expected to send many invitations?
clarifications.a: Yes; recruiters and event attendees, for example. You may not assume a heavy sender is abusive.

clarifications.q: Can you use the invitation note?
clarifications.a: Only to match it against a list of known malicious links, under this exercise's policy.

hints: Separate the exact, cheap check on the send path (a per-sender counter) from the slower, richer scoring that runs on aggregates over hours and days.
A ratio from few invitations is noise. Smooth outcome rates toward a population prior and weigh them by how many invitations have actually been answered.
Abuse that stays under every per-account limit shows up only across accounts. Think about which shared signals group accounts without exposing anyone's data.
followups: Walk through the send path: where is the weekly counter, how is it kept exact across devices, and what happens when its store is unavailable?
Which three aggregate signals carry the most weight, and how is each defined (window, denominator, treatment of pending invitations)?
A ring of new accounts each sends just under the weekly limit. How do you find it, and what do you do to accounts you are less sure about?
How do you measure the false-positive rate of your actions when most restricted members never appeal?
One member receives invitations from 30 newly created accounts in a day. What protects them, and how quickly?

rules.ask: A new member sends 40 invitations; 3 are accepted after a day and the rest are pending. What is their acceptance rate in your design, and why?
The counter shard for some members is lost for two hours. Do those members get unlimited invitations, none, or something else?
Where do your training labels come from, and how do you stop the model learning that recruiters are abusive?
What exactly does the member see, how do they appeal, and how long until a person looks at it?
A whole university shares one network address. How does your cross-account signal avoid flagging every student on it?

incidents: After a large careers fair, 8,000 new graduates each send dozens of invitations to people they just met. Recipients are slow to respond, outcome rates look poor, the detector restricts all 8,000 in one day, and the appeals overwhelm the {{reviewers}} reviewers.

A ring of 30,000 accounts created over two weeks, a small share of the {{new_accounts}} created each day, each sends just under {{weekly_limit}} invitations a week. No per-account limit ever trips, and members' complaints about unknown senders double.
A shard of the store holding weekly counters fails over to a replica that is two hours behind. For those senders the counter reads low, and some send several times the limit before it catches up.
A change to the "don't know" button doubles how often recipients press it. Every sender's score drifts upward overnight and warnings rise tenfold, with no change in sender behaviour.

templates.title: Newsletter issues and notification delivery: digests, unsubscribes honoured everywhere, delivery and open metrics
templates.subtopic: fan-out, preferences, deduplication, delivery metrics

channels: in-app notifications, mobile push and email

sections.scenario: Members and company pages on a professional network publish newsletters; other members subscribe. About {{issues_daily}} issues are published a day, and the largest newsletter has {{largest}} subscribers. When an issue is published, subscribers are told through {{channels}}. Members can choose a daily or weekly digest instead of one message per issue, and they can unsubscribe from a newsletter from the issue page, from their settings on any device, or with an unsubscribe link in the email. Authors see delivery and engagement figures for each issue. A member receives at most {{daily_cap}} newsletter notifications a day under this exercise's rule; the rest wait for the next digest.
sections.problem: Design the delivery system and its metrics. Cover the subscription and preference store, fan-out of one issue to every subscriber, digests, the per-member daily cap, quiet hours in the member's time zone, deduplication across channels (a member who already read the issue in the app), retries without duplicates, unsubscribes that take effect on every channel at once, and the delivery and engagement figures authors see: what is measured, what is an estimate, and what is never shown to them.
sections.constraints: An unsubscribe must stop every channel before the next send to that member, whichever channel it came from. An issue edit or correction must not reach a member before the issue it corrects. Email providers throttle senders that send too fast or draw complaints. Authors see aggregates only: they never see which member opened, clicked or unsubscribed. The largest newsletter's issue should reach all its subscribers within two hours of publishing.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, caps and timings are hypothetical, and the daily cap is this exercise's rule. Email open tracking with a remote image is a widely used and widely known to be imprecise technique: some mail clients load images automatically and some block them.
sections.criteria: One subscription and preference store read at send time; fan-out partitioned by subscriber, isolated by newsletter size, with idempotent sends keyed by issue, member and channel; unsubscribe that takes effect across channels before the next send; ordering so corrections follow the issue they correct; digests, caps and quiet hours with stated precedence; cross-channel deduplication with its latency; separate streams and limits for critical mail; metrics that separate observed from estimated, with opens labelled as estimates; aggregate-only author figures with minimum group sizes; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does the in-app notification count toward the daily cap?
clarifications.a: Yes, every notification about a newsletter counts; the issue itself stays readable in the app.

clarifications.q: What is a "delivery" for email?
clarifications.a: Accepted by the receiving mail server. Whether it reached the inbox is not known.

clarifications.q: Should a member who reads the issue in the app still get the email?
clarifications.a: Your call; say how you know they read it and how late that knowledge can arrive.

clarifications.q: Can authors see their subscriber list?
clarifications.a: Not in this exercise; they see counts and aggregates.

clarifications.q: How quickly must an unsubscribe in one channel reach the others?
clarifications.a: Before the next send to that member on any channel.

hints: Fan-out is a batch per issue, partitioned by subscriber, with every send keyed by (issue, member, channel) so a retry finds the earlier attempt.
Read the preference and subscription state at send time, not at fan-out time; a fan-out for a large newsletter takes long enough for members to change their minds.
Separate the figures you observe (sends, provider acceptances, bounces, clicks through your own links) from those you estimate (opens), and label them that way for authors.
followups: Walk through one issue of the {{largest}}-subscriber newsletter from publish to the last member: partitions, rate limits, and how you know it finished.
A member unsubscribes using the email link while the fan-out for the next issue is half done. Which channels can still reach them, and how do you close that gap?
How do digests interact with the daily cap of {{daily_cap}}, quiet hours and a member who switches from per-issue to weekly mid-week?
Define "open rate" for authors. What is in the numerator and denominator, and what changes when mail clients load images automatically?
How would you show authors an engagement breakdown (for example by subscribers' industry) without letting them single out a member?

rules.ask: The largest newsletter and a thousand small ones publish in the same minute. How do you stop the large fan-out from delaying all the small ones?
The email provider times out after accepting a message. Your retry sends it again. How does your key stop a duplicate in the member's inbox?
Opens jump 25 points overnight for every newsletter. What changed, and what do you tell authors?
The preference store is read at fan-out time. A member unsubscribes after their send was queued. Do they get the issue?
A member travels and their device reports a new time zone; their settings say another. Which one sets quiet hours?

incidents: A member unsubscribes with the email link. The unsubscribe updates email preferences only; the next issue still notifies them in the app, and they report the newsletter as spam.
The {{largest}}-subscriber newsletter publishes an issue and a correction 30 minutes later. The fan-out for the original takes six hours; members late in the fan-out receive the correction first.
A widely used mail client starts loading images automatically. Reported open rates rise by 25 points overnight for every newsletter, and authors start changing what they write in response.
A retry bug resends the same issue email three times to 400,000 members. Complaint rates rise, and an email provider throttles all of the network's mail, including password resets.

templates.title: Hiring analytics for employers: postings to hires across sources, promoted-job spend, candidate privacy kept
templates.subtopic: attribution across sources, late outcomes, spend, aggregate privacy

sections.scenario: About {{employers}} employers post jobs on a professional network. Candidates reach a posting through {{sources}} sources: search, saved-search alerts, a promoted placement the employer paid for, the employer's company page, a shared link, an outside job board, and others. Some apply on the network; others are sent to the employer's own careers site. Employers who connect their applicant tracking system send status updates for applicants (screened, interviewed, offered, hired, rejected, withdrawn), typically up to {{ats_lag}} after the application. Promoted postings are charged under this exercise's pricing per click on the posting, against a daily budget. Employers want a dashboard and an export: from postings to views, applications and hires, by source and over time, with what they spent and what it bought, and how they compare with similar employers.
sections.problem: Design the hiring analytics platform. Cover the events and their keys, joining views, applications and tracking-system updates into one applicant journey, how a hire is credited to sources when a candidate came through several, spend and cost per application and per hire, how figures change when outcomes arrive {{ats_lag}} later and how that is shown, peer benchmarks, and the privacy rules: what an employer may see about its own applicants, what it may see only as aggregates of at least {{min_group}} people, and what it may never see.
sections.constraints: Each employer sees only its own data; a benchmark against similar employers may use only aggregates across at least ten employers. Breakdowns of applicants or viewers by attributes such as region, seniority or skills are shown only for groups of at least {{min_group}} people, and never by protected traits. Members who viewed but did not apply are never identified to the employer. Charges for promoted postings must reconcile exactly with invoices. A member who deletes their account must disappear from every breakdown within this exercise's deadline of 30 days.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, prices, lags and thresholds are hypothetical, and the pricing model is this exercise's rule. Tracking-system updates arrive through an integration that maps each system's statuses to the platform's statuses.
sections.criteria: Journey facts keyed by posting and member with source touches; outcomes as a restatable status history with explicit as-of reporting; a written, versioned attribution rule shown to employers; spend reconciled with invoices including later credits; status mapping per tracking system validated against expected distributions; tenant isolation; aggregate breakdowns with minimum group sizes that also hold under differencing (fixed dimensions, suppression of complementary cells, or noise), and benchmarks with minimum employer counts; deletion propagated through aggregates; no identification of viewers and no protected traits; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: A candidate saw the posting through a promoted placement, then applied a week later from an alert. Which source gets the hire?
clarifications.a: That is your attribution rule to define. Employers want one number per source, and they want to know how it was computed.

clarifications.q: Are hires only known from the tracking system?
clarifications.a: Yes. Employers without an integration see applications but no hires.

clarifications.q: Are clicks from automated traffic charged?
clarifications.a: Clicks later found to be invalid are credited back, sometimes after the invoice.

clarifications.q: Can an employer see its applicants individually?
clarifications.a: Yes, the ones who applied to it, in its own applicant view. The analytics breakdowns are aggregates.

clarifications.q: How are "similar employers" chosen?
clarifications.a: By industry, size band and region; you decide the rule and the minimum.

hints: Model the applicant journey as facts keyed by (posting, member) with touches by source, and outcomes as a slowly arriving, restatable status history.
Attribution is a rule over touches before the application; write it down, version it, and let the dashboard name it.
Minimum group sizes protect one report; two overlapping reports can still be subtracted. Think about every way an employer can slice the same population.
followups: Walk through one hire: which events, with which keys, joined how, and when the hire first appears on the dashboard.
A hire is reported {{ats_lag}} after the application, after last quarter's report was exported. Does last quarter's cost per hire change? How do employers see that?
Invalid clicks are credited back after an invoice. How do spend, the invoice and cost per application stay consistent?

An employer filters a breakdown to one region and then to one region and one seniority. How do you prevent the difference between two allowed reports from revealing a group smaller than {{min_group}}?
How do you build the peer benchmark so no single employer's figures can be worked out from it?

rules.ask: A candidate clicked a promoted placement, then applied from a free alert. Under your rule, what did the promoted spend buy, and is the employer misled?
An employer's finance team exported last quarter's numbers. A month later hires are added. What do they see, and can they reproduce the export?
Two reports each pass your minimum but differ by three people. What stops an employer subtracting one from the other?
What is the grain of your main fact table, and how does a tracking-system status change, arriving weeks later, land in it?
A member deletes their account. Which tables and aggregates change, and what happens to a benchmark already computed?

incidents: After an upgrade of one tracking system, its integration maps "rejected" to "hired". Hires triple for 400 postings across 30 employers, cost per hire on promoted postings falls to a third, and two employers raise their promoted budgets on the strength of it.

An employer exports applicants by region and by region and seniority on the same day. Subtracting one from the other leaves a group of two people in a small office, below the {{min_group}} minimum, and a hiring manager recognises who they are.

Invalid-click detection credits back 8% of one month's promoted clicks after invoices were sent. The dashboard's spend now disagrees with the invoices, and cost per application differs between the export and the dashboard.
An outside job board's referral parameter is dropped by a redirect change; applications from it are recorded as "direct", and that source's share of hires falls to near zero over {{ats_lag}}.

templates.title: An evolving skills taxonomy: free-text skills mapped to standard skills, splits and merges, comparable trend reports
templates.subtopic: versioned taxonomies, entity mapping, crosswalks, consistent time series

sections.scenario: Members of a professional network add skills to their profiles as free text in {{languages}} languages; job postings list required skills; learning courses are tagged with the skills they teach. A taxonomy of about {{standard_skills}} standard skills gives them a common vocabulary, and about {{variants}} distinct free-text strings are mapped to it. The taxonomy is released {{release}}: new skills are added, a broad skill is split into narrower ones, near-duplicates are merged, and some skills are retired. Job matching, course tagging and published trend reports ("fastest-growing skills in a region", "skills most requested in postings") all depend on it.
sections.problem: Design the taxonomy and mapping platform. Cover how the taxonomy and its releases are stored, how free-text strings are mapped to standard skills (and who or what decides), what a split, a merge and a retirement do to existing mappings, how consumers (matching, course tagging, reports) pin or follow releases, and how trend reports stay comparable across releases. Say what a member sees on their own profile when the mapping behind their skill changes.
sections.constraints: A member's profile shows what the member entered; a remapping must never change their profile text or add a skill they did not choose. A member who removes a skill must stop being matched on it within a day. Published trend reports are aggregates over at least 100 members per cell and never broken down by protected traits. A trend over 24 months must not show a jump caused only by a taxonomy release.
sections.assumptions: All counts and cadences are hypothetical. The mapping of free text can combine exact dictionaries, a model you are given, and human curation; how a model scores candidates is not part of this exercise.
sections.criteria: Stable, never-reused skill ids; releases as data with explicit change records; crosswalks that let counts move between releases; trend reports computed in one stated release with history restated, and release effects separated from behaviour; member text, mapping, release and confidence kept separately so remaps never change profiles; split handling that admits ambiguity (keep the parent, ask, or weight by evidence); consumers pinned to releases with a migration window; mapping quality monitored with curated samples per language; removals propagated to matching within the deadline; aggregate reports with minimum cells and no protected traits; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: When a skill is split, which child does a member's existing skill map to?
clarifications.a: Often you cannot tell from the text alone; say what you do when the evidence is not there.

clarifications.q: Do job postings and member profiles use the same release?
clarifications.a: They should when matched; today some consumers lag a release behind.

clarifications.q: Are trend reports ever restated?
clarifications.a: Your decision; readers compare this month with last year's report.

clarifications.q: Who curates the taxonomy?
clarifications.a: A small team of editors approves changes; mappings for the long tail of strings are automatic.

clarifications.q: Can a mapping be wrong?
clarifications.a: Yes; ambiguous strings and abbreviations are common, and the same string can mean different skills in different languages or occupations.

hints: Give every standard skill a stable id that is never reused, and store releases as data: each release is a set of skills plus explicit change records (added, split into, merged into, retired).
A crosswalk between releases (old id → new ids with weights or rules) lets any count be expressed in any release; trend reports pick one release and restate history in it.
Keep the member's text, the mapping, and the mapping's release and confidence as separate fields, so a remap never touches what the member wrote.
followups: Walk through a split of one broad skill into three narrower ones: what changes in the taxonomy, in member mappings, in postings and in last year's trend figures?
Two consumers are pinned to different releases and a merge happens. How does matching between a posting and a member still work during the transition?
How do you decide that a new free-text string deserves its own standard skill rather than a mapping to an existing one, and how fast can that reach reports?
How would you show that this month's "fastest-growing skills" report reflects members' behaviour and not your release?
A mapping is found to have been wrong for a year. What do you correct, what do you restate, and what do you tell report readers?

rules.ask: You update a skill's row in place when it is merged. What do last year's reports and a consumer pinned to the old release see now?
The model maps "PM" to project management for members who meant product management. How do you find that, and who fixes it?
A skill split into three in the last release. In your crosswalk, how is one member's old skill counted under the new release?
Restating 24 months of reports under each release costs how much, and how often? What do you precompute?
A skill's count rises 40% in a month. Name two causes that are not member behaviour, and how your report rules each out.

incidents: A {{release}} release splits a popular skill into three. The next trend report shows the parent skill falling 70% and all three children among the fastest-growing skills in every region.

A mapping update sends a common abbreviation to the wrong standard skill across {{languages}} languages; for six weeks, about 2 million members are matched to postings for a different occupation and recruiters see them in the wrong searches.
Course tagging is pinned one release behind job postings. After a merge, recommendations of courses for the merged skill drop to zero for members who list it.
Members who remove a skill keep receiving job matches for it for nine days, because the matching index reads a nightly snapshot of mappings that is only rebuilt when a release ships.

templates.title: A feature request that would infer something members never chose to share
templates.subtopic: saying no well, reshaping a request, decision rights

request: a score of how likely each member is to be looking for a new job, inferred from their activity and shown to recruiters
an estimate of each member's current salary, inferred from title, location and tenure and shown to recruiters searching for candidates
a flag on members likely to leave their employer soon, offered to that employer's own talent team
requester: a product director with a launch planned next quarter
the sales team, on behalf of a large customer
your own manager, who has already mentioned it to leadership

sections.scenario: Your team owns the data pipelines and features built from member activity on a professional network: profile edits, job views, applications, searches, connections and message metadata. Members can already state some things about themselves, such as that they are open to new roles, and choose who sees that. You receive a request from {{requester}}: build {{request}}. The requester has a business case and wants it live in {{weeks}} weeks. Members have not chosen to share this, and most would not expect it to be computed about them.
sections.problem: How do you respond? Cover how you understand the goal behind the request, how you assess the harm to members if the inference is right, if it is wrong, and if it leaks, who else must be involved and who decides, what you propose instead, and how you communicate your position to the requester and to your own team. Then tell me about a real time you pushed back on, or reshaped, a request to use data in a way the people it described would not expect, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You do not own the product decision or the privacy policy. The pipeline could technically compute the inference in a few weeks. The requester's goal is legitimate: recruiters want to reach people who are open to being reached.
sections.assumptions: The situation is hypothetical. Nothing here describes any company's real products, models or policies.
sections.criteria: Starts from the goal and asks questions before judging; assesses harm concretely (wrong inferences, correct inferences shown to the wrong audience, especially an employer, leaks, members' expectations) rather than only legality; brings in product, privacy and legal owners with clear facts and respects decision rights; proposes alternatives that serve the goal with members' choice (member-stated signals, controls on who sees them, aggregates for planning); communicates a firm position respectfully, with evidence, and escalates fairly if needed; real example with personal contribution and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the inference legal?
clarifications.a: You do not know; the privacy and legal teams would need to review it. Legal is not the same as acceptable to members.

clarifications.q: Would members be able to see or correct it?
clarifications.a: The request does not say. It assumes they would not see it.

clarifications.q: How accurate would it be?
clarifications.a: Nobody has measured it. A quick prototype by an analyst suggests it is right more often than chance, with many errors.

clarifications.q: Is there already a way for members to state this?
clarifications.a: For job-seeking, yes; for salary and leaving intent, only partly.

hints: Separate the goal (what the requester actually needs) from the proposed means (an inference about members).
Think about who is harmed by a wrong inference, and who by a right one shown to the wrong person.
A good "no" usually comes with a better "yes": something that serves the goal with members' choice built in.
followups: Walk me through your first conversation with the requester. What do you ask before you say anything about the request itself?
Who must be involved in the decision, in what order, and what do you bring them?
The requester says competitors already do this and the launch is committed. What do you do?
What alternative would you propose, and how would you show it serves the same goal?
In your real example, what did you personally do, and what happened to the working relationship?

rules.ask: Most members will never opt in. The requester says that makes the feature worthless. What do you answer?
The privacy review says it is allowed with a notice in the policy. Is that the end of the question for you?
The recruiter needs to reach individual people. Which part of the goal does an aggregate still serve?
The requester escalates to your director, who asks why the team is blocking revenue. What do you put in front of the director?
What did you personally decide or say, and to whom?

templates.title: An engineer on the team who is underperforming
templates.subtopic: feedback, expectations, support, fairness to the team

symptom: pull requests that sit for weeks and come back with the same review comments each time
on-call incidents in the job-alert pipeline that teammates have had to re-handle after the hand-off
estimates missed by a factor of three on every task this quarter, discovered only at the deadline
your_role: the team's tech lead, not the engineer's manager

sections.scenario: You work on a team that runs the pipelines behind job alerts and job recommendations on a professional network. One engineer, on the team for {{tenure}}, has been struggling for about two months: {{symptom}}. Teammates have started working around them and one has complained to you privately. You are {{your_role}}. The engineer has not raised anything with you.
sections.problem: How do you handle it? Cover how you check what is actually happening before you act, the first conversation (what you say, what you ask, what you avoid), how you set clear expectations and support, how you keep the rest of the team working well meanwhile, what you do if things do not improve, and who else you involve and when. Then tell me about a real time you helped someone who was struggling at work, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The engineer's work is needed for a commitment due next month. You may not share the engineer's situation with the rest of the team. If you are not the manager, you have no formal authority over the engineer's performance review.
sections.assumptions: The situation is hypothetical. There may be causes you do not know about.
sections.criteria: Gathers specific evidence before acting and separates it from second-hand complaints; holds a private, direct and respectful first conversation that asks before telling and does not speculate about personal causes; sets clear, measurable expectations with support and a check-in date; adapts fairly to personal circumstances (time, scope, available support) without lowering the bar indefinitely; keeps the team and the commitment healthy without exposing the engineer; involves the manager or people team at the right time and acts within their role; real example with what helped and what they learned, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Has the engineer had good reviews before?
clarifications.a: Yes; their work was solid until recently.

clarifications.q: Does the engineer know there is a problem?
clarifications.a: Probably in part; nobody has said it to them directly.

clarifications.q: Is there a formal performance process?
clarifications.a: Yes, run by managers with people-team support; it is not the first step.

clarifications.q: Is the complaint from the teammate fair?
clarifications.a: Partly; it is also frustrated and second-hand.

hints: Gather specific, recent examples first; feedback without examples is opinion.
In the first conversation, ask before you tell: there may be a reason you do not know, and it is theirs to share or not.
Clear expectations, support and a check-in date belong together.
followups: What exactly do you say in the first five minutes of the conversation?
The engineer tells you about a difficult personal situation. What changes, and what does not?
Six weeks later, there is little improvement. What do you do next, and who do you involve?
How do you protect next month's commitment without making the engineer's situation visible to the team?
In your real example, what did you do that helped, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: Why involve them at that point rather than earlier or later, and what do you still own yourself?
What does reassigning the work tell the engineer and the team, and how do you say it?
Give me one piece of feedback exactly as you would say it to them.
How do you support them without asking for details they have not offered, and without lowering the bar for everyone?
What did you personally say or do?

templates.title: Raising a risk your manager does not want to hear
templates.subtopic: risk evidence, options, escalation without surprise

risk: the new recruiter candidate-search index cannot meet its latency target at the launch's expected load
the member data export built for privacy requests misses two downstream stores that hold member data
the migration of profile history will not finish before the old store's support contract ends
manager_state: has just told leadership the work is on track
is new and under pressure to show quick wins
has twice said 'let's not raise problems without solutions'

sections.scenario: You lead the technical work on a project for a professional network that is due in {{weeks}} weeks. You have found that {{risk}}. You raised it informally with your manager, who {{manager_state}}. Their response was that it would probably work out and that you should keep going. You believe the risk is real and that the longer it goes unspoken, the fewer options the team will have.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover how you make the risk concrete and checkable, how you prepare options rather than only a problem, how you raise it again with your manager, when and how it goes further if your manager still disagrees, and how you keep the working relationship. Then tell me about a real time you raised a risk that someone above you did not want to hear, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Your manager decides what is reported to leadership. You are not willing to stay silent about something that could harm members or the launch. Other teams depend on the date.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Makes the risk concrete with evidence and stated assumptions; brings options with costs and a recommendation; raises it again with the manager directly and constructively, acknowledging their pressures; distinguishes risks to members (privacy, correctness) from risks to a date and escalates the former without delay; escalates beyond the manager only transparently, telling the manager first, through a legitimate forum; records the risk in writing in a way that helps decisions; keeps the relationship intact and supports the decision once made unless it harms members; real example with personal actions and outcome, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: How sure are you?
clarifications.a: You have a test or analysis that shows it, but it rests on assumptions someone could challenge.

clarifications.q: Is there any way to still meet the date?
clarifications.a: Possibly, with reduced scope or more people; you have not costed either.

clarifications.q: Who else knows?
clarifications.a: One engineer on your team who helped with the analysis.

clarifications.q: Is there a regular forum where risks are reported?
clarifications.a: A weekly status review; your manager presents it.

hints: Turn a worry into evidence: what you measured, the assumption it depends on, and how you would know if you are wrong.
Bring options with costs (cut scope, add people, move the date, accept the risk with a mitigation) and a recommendation.
Going above your manager is sometimes right; doing it without telling them almost never is.
followups: How would you present the risk to your manager the second time, and what is different from the first?
Your manager still says to keep going. What do you do next, and how do you tell them?
What is the difference for you between a risk to the date and a risk to members, and does it change what you do?
The risk materialises two weeks before the launch. What do you do, and what do you say about the earlier conversations?
In your real example, how did you raise it, what happened, and what did it do to the relationship?

rules.ask: Does your manager know you are doing that? What exactly do you tell them beforehand?
Your manager challenges the main assumption behind your analysis. How do you settle it quickly?
Which option would you recommend, and what does it cost the people who depend on the date?
How do you write it down so it informs rather than reads as covering yourself?
What did you personally say, to whom, and when?

templates.title: A high-visibility new project versus finishing an important, unglamorous one
templates.subtopic: finishing work, opportunity cost, team motivation

new_project: a writing assistant for recruiters' outreach messages, with a launch demo already planned
a new analytics dashboard for creators that leadership wants to show at a public event
a skills-based job matching prototype that two directors are excited about
unglamorous: the migration that lets a member's account deletion reach every derived table
retiring the fragile job-ingestion pipeline that pages the team every week
the backfill that makes skills trend reports comparable across taxonomy releases

sections.scenario: Your team on a professional network is {{remaining}} of work away from finishing {{unglamorous}}. Nobody outside the team asks about it, but it matters: members, on-call engineers or report readers depend on it. You are now offered the chance to lead {{new_project}}. It would need most of the team, it is highly visible, and several engineers are excited about it. If the team takes it, the unfinished work stops.
sections.problem: How do you decide, and how do you lead the team through the decision? Cover how you weigh the cost of stopping the unfinished work (including what happens to it half done), how you test whether the new project really needs the team now, what options sit between all or nothing, how you present the choice to the people who offered the project, and how you keep the team motivated whichever way it goes. Then tell me about a real time you chose between visible new work and finishing something important, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot staff both at full speed. Your manager will support either choice if it is well argued. Half-finished migrations and backfills have costs of their own.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Quantifies what the unfinished work protects and the cost of pausing it (risk, toil, half-migrated state), not only its remaining effort; tests what the new project truly needs by its date; considers options between all or nothing and states their costs; recommends clearly and explains it to the sponsors with evidence; leads the team through the decision, addressing disappointment and making the less visible work valued; real example with the decision, its cost and lessons, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the new project's date fixed?
clarifications.a: The demo date is; what must be ready by then is negotiable.

clarifications.q: What does the unfinished work protect?
clarifications.a: Say what you think it protects in your setting; the scenario names the work, not its exact consequences.

clarifications.q: How does the team feel?
clarifications.a: Some engineers want the new project; the two who know the unfinished work best want to finish it.

clarifications.q: Could another team take one of them?
clarifications.a: Possibly, with a hand-off cost.

hints: Write down what each option costs and what it protects, including the cost of leaving work half done.
Ask what the new project needs by its date, not what it could use.
Options between all or nothing (a small team for the new work, a finish-first plan with a date, a hand-off) are usually better than either extreme.
followups: How would you estimate the cost of pausing the unfinished work for three months?
What would you say to the directors who offered the project if your recommendation is to finish first?
The engineers who want the new project are disappointed by your decision. What do you do?
You split the team, and both pieces of work slip. What do you change?
In your real example, what did you decide, what did it cost, and would you choose the same again?

rules.ask: Which work slips when both are under-staffed, and who did you tell in advance?
The demo goes ahead without your team and goes badly. What do you say?
What does the receiving team need in order to own the unfinished work safely, and how long does that take?
How do you make the unglamorous work visible and valued for the engineers who stay on it?
What did you personally recommend, and to whom?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a professional network of members, recruiters and companies
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, redesign for member-controlled visibility

angle: the data model and why it held up
the hardest correctness problem you solved
the most important reliability decision you made
requirement: each member's visibility settings decide who may see each field
a member's account deletion reaches every derived table and search index
recruiters see a member only as that member allows
figures about companies are released only for groups above a minimum size

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or customers depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change if its data described {{members}} members of a professional network, read by three audiences with different rights (members themselves, recruiters and companies), and it had to guarantee that {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes if the data described {{members}} members and the system had to guarantee that {{requirement}}: where the rule is enforced, what each audience can read, what derived data must change, and how you would show the guarantee holds. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The professional-network setting is hypothetical and describes general techniques, not how any company builds its systems.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; an honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible redesign for the requirement that follows data into every copy, index and aggregate, enforces the rule at read time and at copy time, handles changes of mind and deletions with propagation and verification, and recognises that hashing is not anonymisation; a way to test the guarantee continuously; own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a data system?
clarifications.a: It should move, store or compute data that others depend on; a service with a significant data model counts.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: Do I need to know privacy law?
clarifications.a: No. Reason about who may see what, where that is enforced and how you would test it.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the requirement, follow the data from where it is written to every place it is copied, indexed or aggregated; each copy is a place the rule must hold.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Where in your system would you enforce the guarantee that {{requirement}}, and what happens to copies made before a member changes their mind?
How would you test that guarantee continuously, not just once?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
A member changes a setting. How long until every copy in your design respects it, and how do you know?
Could someone with your output and one public profile re-identify a member? How do you know?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
Is the check made where the data is read, or where it is copied? What happens to an export made yesterday?
